cia-0000119206:
Also from November 1968, this CIA document lists locations of four camps holding American, Thai, and Philippine prisoners in Laos. The heading breaks off at the start of that word four, but a companion document from the same month covers the same ground. Together they map one corner of the Laos camp system.

Camp locations were working knowledge for anyone planning rescues or tracking the missing. In Laos, where the war was officially secret, even basic facts about prisoners were hard won. The document preserves the agency's map of those four sites as its sources described them. It was part of the long effort to account for allied men held beyond Vietnam's borders.
cia-0000119706:
A February 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Egypt. The 1952 revolution had ended the monarchy, and Generals Naguib and Nasser were circling each other for control of the new state. Within two years Nasser would push Naguib aside and rule alone.

The paper tries to read that contest and Egypt's likely course. Egypt was the Arab world's largest state, and its direction shaped the whole region's politics. For readers, the forecast is a snapshot of judgment at a hinge moment. It was made when the revolution's winner was not yet clear, and its long rule over Egypt still lay in the future.
cia-0000124306: A November 1950 CIA document reports on American prisoners of war at Mukden and Erhmienpa, holding sites in Manchuria. The Korean War was then five months old, and the prisoner question was only beginning. The paper records some of the earliest traces of captured men. Early traces were precious because the first winter of captivity was the deadliest, and any confirmed location gave the tracing effort a place to begin asking questions.
cia-0000132306: Jordan denying a breach of the United Nations arms embargo leads Situation Report 616. The report belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series and is dated January 4, 1991. Its headline breaks off after the denial. Jordan sat caught between Iraq and the coalition and had to walk a careful line. The short report records the denial as part of the daily political watch on the crisis.
cia-0000132606: Relations between Yugoslavia and Cuba fill item 1 of a CIA general series dated July 1, 1960. Tito's Yugoslavia followed its own course inside the communist world, apart from Moscow. Havana courted Belgrade as one more patron standing outside the Kremlin's shadow. The short item covers that relationship and what each side hoped to gain from it.
cia-0000135806: A cable asking for guidance fills a CIA record dated May 1, 1954. The cable went to a senior representative whose name was deleted before release. Requests of this kind form the paper trail of command in a covert campaign. The field was asking headquarters what to do next in Guatemala. The short record keeps the request as it was sent that spring.
cia-0000136006: From 6 February 1954 comes a CIA routing sheet, since declassified, on courier and pouch information, carried on a routing sheet with a cable from Lincoln attached. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136206: A CIA cable dated 6 May 1954 deals with the availability of F-47 planes, called critical to the operation in the cable's own heading, in files since declassified. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
un-ga-res-106:
Armenian deaths under the Ottoman Empire stand at the heart of the text filed here as Resolution 106. The file is not a UN text at all. It is a resolution of the U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 106 of the 110th Congress, sent to committee on 30 January 2007. It calls on the President to make sure that U.S. foreign dealings show due grasp of the facts on human rights, ethnic cleansing, and genocide in the U.S. record on the Armenian Genocide.

Adam Schiff led the sponsors of the text, with men of both parties beside him. The short name is given in full: the Affirmation of the United States Record on the Armenian Genocide Resolution. Fights over such texts, and over the word genocide itself, marked U.S. and Turkish ties for years. The catalog's UN label and 1915 year are both wrong.
un-sc-res-106:
Resolution 106 condemns an attack by Israeli regular army forces on Egyptian forces in the Gaza Strip on 28 February 1955. The catalog record dates the entry 1948, but the text itself was adopted on 29 March 1955, by a unanimous vote. An Egypt-Israel armistice panel had found the attack was planned and ordered by Israeli authorities.

The Council calls the attack a breach of the cease-fire terms in Resolution 54 and of the General Armistice Agreement between Egypt and Israel. It calls on Israel to take all steps needed to stop such actions. It also warns that any willful breach of the armistice puts the deal at risk, and that no real peace in Palestine can come unless both sides keep their word.
un-sc-res-1406: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1406, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 2002. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1506:
Libya's long isolation ended at the United Nations with Resolution 1506, adopted in September 2003. Sanctions placed on Tripoli after the Lockerbie bombing had been suspended for years. Once Libya accepted responsibility terms and a settlement, the Council lifted the measures for good.

Inside the short text, the members remove the arms and travel bans and close the sanctions committee's work. The vote closed a dispute that had run since the 1980s over the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. It remains the formal end of one of the UN's longest sanctions cases.
un-sc-res-1606: Security Council Resolution 1606 is preserved here from the UN's official record, in a transcription by English Wikisource. Resolutions like this one typically run a few pages: findings first, then a short list of decisions. The entry's completeness is its feature, giving the whole act rather than a headline version of what was decided.
un-sc-res-1706:
Darfur's suffering drove Resolution 1706, adopted in August 2006. The Council voted to expand the UN mission in Sudan to take over from African Union troops in Darfur. Sudan's government, however, refused to accept the deployment, setting up a long standoff.

The text details a force of more than 17,000 soldiers plus police, tasked with protecting civilians and guarding the Darfur peace deal. Because Khartoum blocked it, the plan was later replaced by a joint UN-African Union mission. The resolution preserves the world's first full answer to Darfur, and the limits of voting without consent.
un-sc-res-1806: Resolution 1806, adopted in 2008, is a Security Council act preserved here through English Wikisource's transcription of the record. The number places it among the Council's 1800s run, the output of its later-2000s sessions. The entry gives the full decision at that place: grounds, orders, and the reporting follow-through that such texts standardly require.
cia-0000132506:
Two weeks into Kennedy's presidency, on February 4, 1961, the CIA produced this briefing on Cuba. An exile invasion force was taking shape, and the agency was gathering the intelligence to support it. Cuba reporting was being written for men weighing an attack.

Papers like this one tracked the island's politics and defenses during the run-up to the Bay of Pigs. Several Cuba briefings carry the same February 4 date, a sign of how fast the reporting cycle had become. Preserved from the CIA Reading Room, the text lets readers sit inside that pre-invasion information stream.
cia-0000136706: Dated 6 February 1961, a Spanish document from the declassified files of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in final training, its April landing in Cuba about ten weeks off. The catalog gives this item no subject heading. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the brigade's February records from the operation's last stretch of preparation.
plos-pone-0000006:
Qizhou Lian and co-authors reported in 2006 on a search for cells that could seed new blood vessels. Working with mouse embryonic stem cells, they grew embryoid bodies, small clumps that mimic early development. Inside them they hunted for a rare cell type marked by high CD9 and no SSEA-1.

From single cells of that type, the team raised clonal lines, families of identical cells. Those lines showed endothelial-like potential, meaning they could act like the cells that line blood vessels. A clean, copyable source of such cells matters for studying vessel growth and, one day, for repair work in damaged tissue. The study maps how to find and grow them.
cia-0000136306: Cable from Lincoln for Cadick and Broadfrost an Order: re Strike Mission is a declassified CIA cable dated 1954. The catalog title is unusually informative for this series: a sender signing as Lincoln, two recipients named Cadick and Broadfrost, and a message that gives an order about a strike mission. Names of that style were the working code names used inside agency traffic. The catalog adds nothing about the mission or its outcome. The cable survives as a brief piece of operational traffic, released through the CIA Reading Room.
moyle-institutes-justinian-1906:
Emperor Justinian ordered the Institutes in 533 as a first textbook for law students in the Roman Empire. J. B. Moyle's English translation, in the 1906 edition used here, made the short work a staple for students of Roman law. Justinian's compilers built it on older teaching books, chiefly the one by Gaius.

Four books lay out the law in order: persons and their status, property and wills, promises and wrongs, and how suits are brought. The style is brisk and plain, since new students had to grasp the whole map at once. Civil law systems across Europe and beyond grew from this frame, so the book still earns study.
wieger-textes-philosophiques-1906:
Léon Wieger, a French Jesuit who spent his life in China, gathered these Chinese philosophical texts in 1906 and presented them in French. Wieger ran a mission press in Hebei and became known for exact work on Chinese language and thought. His aim was to let French readers meet China's sages in their own words.

The chosen pieces span schools and ages, from early masters to later teachers of the Way and of Confucius. Short lives and notes help the reader place each text. Wieger's versions were trusted for their care, and the set still serves as a window on how Europe first read Chinese thought in depth.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d106: Chiang Kai-shek wrote to Roosevelt on November 9, 1943, and the letter is Document 106 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Chiang was preparing to travel to Cairo, a journey that would take him out of China in wartime for the summit. His letters to Washington that month carried both requests and assurances. The record gives the date and the names. The text in the Foreign Relations series holds the particulars.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d206:
Prime Minister Churchill telegraphed President Roosevelt on 10 November 1943 with a complaint about France. Changes in the French National Committee had left Charles de Gaulle as its sole president, and Churchill says he is not at all content with that outcome.

The body the Allies recognized, he points out, rested on a co-presidency shared by de Gaulle and General Giraud, a body of a totally different character. Churchill suggests that Britain and America keep an attitude of complete reserve toward the new arrangement until he and Roosevelt can discuss the position together. They would soon do so in person at Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d306:
The entry under this title contains no draft text at all, only the editors' note about one. The document it names is an American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 24 November 1943, carrying amendments in President Roosevelt's own handwriting, and preserved in the Roosevelt Papers.

From the note, Harry Hopkins dictated the typed draft to Warrant Officer Cornelius in the solarium of the President's villa. It was the afternoon of 24 November. By Cornelius's later account, Hopkins worked without any prepared notes or papers before him. Roosevelt's handwritten changes on this draft were then worked into the revised version of 25 November, which is printed later in the volume. Readers should note the mismatch: the catalog title promises the draft itself, but only its history is given here.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d406: Harry Hopkins and President Roosevelt exchanged two short handwritten notes at Tehran on 1 December 1943, near the end of that day's luncheon meeting. The scrap, preserved in the Hopkins Papers and printed in facsimile in Sherwood's book, concerns the evening's dinner. Hopkins asks what the President thinks of letting the Russians give dinner that night, calling it his last chance at Russian food. Roosevelt scrawls back his answer underneath: OK, but I have to leave early, as the party sleeps at the camp. The brief exchange is the whole document.

crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-06:

dunsany-time-and-the-gods-1906:

machen-house-of-souls-1906:
Machen's tales of awe and dread stand gathered in The House of Souls of 1906. Its crown is The White People, a girl's diary of rites learned in the Welsh hills. Lovecraft took that tale as his model for the folk horror story.

blackwood-empty-house-1906:
Algernon Blackwood made his name with The Empty House and Other Ghost Stories in 1906. It was his first book of ghost tales. Two tales lead the set. One is The Empty House. The other is A Haunted Island.

arbois-jubainville-druides-1906:
Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville, the head of the French school of Celtic studies, wrote this work in French in 1906. His theme is the druids and the gods of the Celts. The Celts once spread from Ireland to the lands of the Danube.

The book looks hard at Celtic gods who take the shape of beasts. Bulls, boars, horses, and birds each play a part in rite and myth. He set the druids at the heart of that faith, as its priests and wise men. French in tongue, it stays a lead text of its school.
lowell-mars-and-its-canals-1906:
Percival Lowell set out his canal scheme in full grown form in this book of 1906. It rests on eleven more years of watch at his Flagstaff lens since his first Mars book. The lines on Mars had grown in his maps to a vast web of works.

Lowell gives charts, plates, and counts to show the canals are too straight to be a trick of nature. He reads them as the last great work of a race on a world that dries year by year. The book is the high case for a lived in Mars, made by its chief voice.
shahnameh-warner-vol2-1906:
Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, the great epic poem of Persia. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner turned it into English verse. Theirs was the first full English verse version of the whole poem. Book two of their set came out in 1906.

Kings rise and fall in long tales of war, love, and fate. Heroes fight beasts and rival lords while wise men warn of pride. The Warners kept the sweep of the tale in plain, strong verse. For most English readers, this set was the first door into Persia's best loved book.
bibliotheca-chemica-vol-1-1906:
John Ferguson built the Bibliotheca Chemica as a list of one great store. James Young had amassed books on alchemy, chemistry, and drugs for years. Book One of the list came out in 1906. It runs from A to K in the names of the scribes.

Each head gives the full title, date, size, and notes on the book's worth. Rare tracts stand by the great names of the field in one run. Ferguson was a Glasgow chemist with a love of the old books. The list is still a chief tool for all who trace the old chemists.
london-white-fang-1906:
Jack London published White Fang in 1906, a wolfdog's passage from the Yukon wild to domestication. The companion mirror of The Call of the Wild reverses Buck's road: tame blood calls this hero toward the fire. London answered critics who charged him with faking nature by building the tale on careful Klondike observation.

White Fang, three parts wolf, learns the wild's law from his mother Kiche and the famine winters of the Mackenzie country. Gray Beaver, Beauty Smith, and a San Francisco dog pit teach him man's cruelty. Weedon Scott, a mining engineer, tames him with patience and kindness, a method no hand had tried on the fighting wolf. In California White Fang saves Judge Scott from a convict and earns his rest at Sierra Vista. The book's study of heredity and environment made it a school classic.
lagerlof-wonderful-adventures-nils-1906:
Selma Lagerlof published The Wonderful Adventures of Nils in 1906, a children's book written to teach Swedish geography. Nils is a lazy boy who torments animals on his farm. A magic spell shrinks him to tiny size. He flies off on the back of a goose, joining a flock of wild geese.

The flock travels the length of Sweden, from south to far north. Nils learns kindness, courage, and the ways of animals on the way. Folk tales and natural facts fill each stop. Swedish schools used the book for years. It remains a beloved classic, read far beyond Sweden for its charm and wonder.
sherrington-integrative-action-1906:
Charles Sherrington was a British physiologist whose lab work mapped how nerves join muscles into working systems. His 1906 book The Integrative Action of the Nervous System sums up years of trials on reflexes. It is often named the founding text of modern neuroscience.

Sherrington names the synapse, the tiny junction where one nerve cell hands its signal to the next. He shows how reflex arcs combine, compete, and yield so that an animal acts as one whole. Later brain science built directly on his terms, his maps, and his careful method. He coined much of the language that nerve science still speaks.
shaku-sermons-buddhist-abbot-1906:
Soyen Shaku was the Zen abbot who spoke for Buddhism at the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893. His Sermons of a Buddhist Abbot, published in 1906, gathers the addresses he gave on his American tour of 1905 and 1906. His student Suzuki translated them into English.

Shaku explains karma, rebirth, and the Buddha's enlightenment in a calm, gracious voice shaped for Western hearers. He presents Buddhism as a way of waking, not a set of dogmas to be believed on command. The sermons mark the moment Zen first addressed America through one of its own masters. His dignity did much to win Buddhism a fair hearing in America.
atkinson-thought-vibration-1906:
William Walker Atkinson was a Chicago lawyer turned New Thought writer who filled magazines and cheap manuals with his teaching. His Thought Vibration, published in 1906, explains the law of attraction in the mental world. It became New Thought's most circulated manual.

Atkinson teaches that thoughts are vibrations that draw like conditions toward the thinker, as a magnet draws iron filings. shahnama-warner-vol-2-1906:
Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner published Volume 2 of their Shahnama of Firdausi in 1906. The Shahnama, or Book of Kings, is the Persian national epic, written by Firdausi around the year 1000. The Warner brothers set out to give English readers the whole poem, in nine volumes.

Volume 2 carries the epic's early kings and heroes onward, through wars, hunts, and court tales told in verse. Their translation kept the poem's shape while making its stories plain to English readers. No full English Shahnama existed before theirs. The volume continues a vast record of Persian myth and memory, where legend and early history flow together without a clear break.
kropotkin-conquest-bread-1906:
Peter Kropotkin published The Conquest of Bread in 1906, in its English form, as the classic program of anarchist communism. Kropotkin wrote for workers who made everything and owned little. He argued that food, housing, and goods already produced could meet everyone's needs if shared by free agreement.

Chapters plan how a free society would take over bakeries, farms, and workshops and run them without wages or bosses. Kropotkin attacked the wage system as the root of poverty amid plenty. suess-face-of-earth-vol2-sollas-1906:

One of them, the Tethys, became a lasting term of geology from his pages. Sollas's translation kept pace with the German original's ambition. The volume shows geology thinking at planetary scale a generation before plate tectonics gave it a new engine.
ehrlich-collected-studies-immunity-vol1-:

galsworthy-man-of-property-1906:

jonson-volpone-1606:

kipling-puck-of-pooks-hill-1906:

andreyev-savva-and-life-of-man-1906:

lea-inquisition-spain-vol-2-1906:

ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-3-1606:

cartier-memoir-baxter-1906:

mandeville-fable-bees-1806:

gibbs-scientific-papers-vol-1-1906:
J. Willard Gibbs published his core papers during his life, and his Scientific Papers gathered them in 1906. Volume one holds the thermodynamics work, centering on his long paper On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances. Gibbs taught at Yale and worked in near quiet. His math reshaped how scientists treat heat, energy, and chemical change.

The volume presents the phase rule, which predicts how substances in balance behave. It also sets out chemical potential, a key tool for judging reactions. His geometric methods picture these relations in clear shapes. Together the papers founded much of physical chemistry. Few single volumes carry such weight.
gibbs-scientific-papers-vol-2-1906:
Volume two of the Scientific Papers of J. Willard Gibbs, issued in 1906, ranges past thermodynamics. Gibbs wrote on dynamics, the study of motion under forces. He also reshaped vector analysis, the math of quantities with direction. The notation he built for it is the one physics still uses today.

Alongside those works stand his papers on the electromagnetic theory of light. Unpublished fragments close the volume and show his mind still at work. The set pairs with volume one to give his whole output. Readers find a style of rare compression and calm. Almost every page started lines of later research.
spr-proceedings-vol20-1906:
Volume twenty of the Proceedings, from 1906, consists of part fifty three alone. The Society for Psychical Research often filled a whole part with one great report. Telepathy and trance work dominate the society's business in this period. Long sittings with mediums appear in near verbatim form.

Investigators weigh the Piper material and its rivals with care. Spontaneous cases of apparitions arrive in smaller numbers, well documented. The volume's single part format suits readers who want depth over range. It forms one brick in the archive wall built between 1882 and 1930. The society's standards, set early, hold firm here. Evidence first remains the rule.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol06:
In 1859 Volume VI of the Journal of Discourses added another year of preaching to the printed record. Liverpool remained the printing base for a Utah church speaking to a worldwide flock. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles fill the pages, their sermons taken down word for word.

The talks show doctrine being worked out in public, applied to marriages, farms, debts, and doubts. That mix of the sacred and the everyday is the Journal's signature across all twenty-six volumes. Volume VI, read in sequence, lets the movement's teaching be watched as it grows.
bukhari-traditions-islamiques-houdas-mar:
Tome II of Les Traditions Islamiques, printed in 1906, continues Houdas and Marçais's French rendering of al-Bukhari's Sahih. The great hadith collection proceeds book by book through prayer, alms, pilgrimage, trade, and the daily rules of the faith. Each report carries its chain of transmitters, the isnad that guarantees it in Muslim scholarship.

The translators worked under the Imprimerie nationale, and their version stayed standard for French readers of Islam. Tome II holds the middle of the Prophet's example as the tradition preserves it: law, worship, and conduct in reported detail. The set's scale shows the weight Sunni Islam lays on this book.
rivers-the-todas-1906:
W. H. R. Rivers went to the Nilgiri Hills of southern India to study the Toda people, and his 1906 book reports what he found. The Todas were few in number, pastoral, and organized around the buffalo in a way no outsider had fully recorded.

At the center stands the sacred dairy, where buffalo milk is handled as a ritual by priest-dairymen under strict rules. Rivers also documents polyandry, in which brothers share a wife, and works out Toda kinship with new care. His genealogical method, built for this study, changed fieldwork itself. The book launched British social anthropology's classic period.
haddon-magic-and-fetishism-1906:
Alfred Cort Haddon led the Cambridge expedition to the Torres Straits in 1898, a landmark of modern fieldwork. This short 1906 book draws on that work to explain magic and fetishism for general readers, in plain terms.

Haddon defines magic as the attempt to control events by rites and spells, and the fetish as an object believed to hold power. He illustrates both from the islanders he knew, and from reports worldwide. His aim is sympathy as much as theory: to show the logic inside practices Europeans mocked. The book is a compact doorway into early anthropology's central questions.
conrad-mirror-of-sea-1906:
The Mirror of the Sea, published in 1906, is Conrad's book of memoir-essays on the sailing life he had left behind. After twenty years in the merchant service, he wrote of ships and the sea as a man speaks of a lost home.

The essays take up anchors, storms, the character of famous ships, and the fellowship of crews. 'The Fine Art' praises seamanship as a craft of hand and judgment. There is no plot here, only memory refined into prose of great beauty. Sailors and landsmen alike have kept it in print as the classic elegy for the age of sail.
ford-fifth-queen-1906:
The Fifth Queen, published in 1906, opens Ford's trilogy on Katharine Howard, fifth wife of Henry VIII. Katharine comes to a court eaten by faction, a young Howard girl carrying her family's hopes after the Cleves marriage fails.

Ford builds the Tudor court as impressionist theater: whispers, ceremonies, spies, and the slow gears of policy turning behind tapestries. Cromwell watches the new queen rise as his own power thins. The novel prizes atmosphere over pageant, truth of feeling over chronicle. It began Ford's most sustained historical achievement, completed in two further volumes of high quality. Historians praise its feel for the period.
santayana-life-reason-vol-5-1906:
Reason in Science, published in 1906, closes The Life of Reason as its fifth and crowning volume. Santayana turns last to science, the pursuit his whole system had to honor without worshiping.

He treats science as reason's most disciplined form: a method for mapping nature's order, powerful exactly because it describes rather than consoles. Against it he sets the claims of history and of the inner life, which science cannot replace. The volume rounds the five books into one vision: reason as man's one guide in every sphere. Santayana was thirty-nine when he finished; few systems begin so complete.
mctaggart-dogmas-religion-1906:
Some Dogmas of Religion, published in 1906, is McTaggart's fearless examination of what religious belief can survive reason. He takes up dogmas one by one, God, freedom, survival, and the soul, and weighs each from an idealist standpoint.

His results startled readers: he argues against a personal, all-powerful God while defending survival after death and the primacy of love. McTaggart was an atheist who thought religion's emotions truer than its creeds. The book's candor and calm made it notorious in Edwardian Cambridge. It remains one of the most honest works of its kind in English.
dampier-voyages-vol1-1906:
William Dampier, an English buccaneer with a naturalist's eye, circled the globe in the late seventeenth century. Volume One of John Masefield's 1906 edition centers on his A New Voyage Round the World of 1697. Dampier was the first Englishman to explore Australia's coast.

Sailing with pirates in the Pacific, he still found time to note winds, plants, animals, and peoples. His plain, exact style shaped English travel writing and fed Swift and Defoe. Masefield, himself a sailor-poet, edits with love. Dampier's double life, pirate and pioneer of science, makes the volume a lasting pleasure. His word lists for native tongues were among the first printed in English.
dampier-voyages-vol2-1906:
Volume Two of Masefield's edition of Dampier's Voyages continues the buccaneer-naturalist's writings. Dampier's later works include his discourse on trade winds and his voyage to New Holland in 1699. The Royal Navy had by then given the old pirate a ship of his own.

His wind charts served sailors for a century, and his account of Australia's west coast was the first in English. Dampier describes strange animals and plants with a pioneer's patience. Masefield adds the supplement and the remaining voyages to complete the set. The volume shows why scientists, not only sailors, honored Dampier's name.
pothier-obligations-contracts-1806:
Robert Pothier, a French judge and scholar, wrote his Treatise on Obligations in the 1760s. William Evans's English translation of 1806 is the version here, with notes on English law. Pothier's book is the French civilian foundation of modern contract law.

He defines contracts, consent, error, and fault in clear, ordered chapters. His rules passed almost whole into the French civil code and from there worldwide. English and American judges cited the translation in court for decades. Anyone tracing where modern contract ideas came from will land on Pothier, the quiet professor from Orléans who organized a whole field.
plos-pone-0003406:
Yu Sun, Huai Li, and Ying Liu compared gene activity in stem cells across species in 2008. Embryonic stem cells can turn into many cell types as an embryo grows. Genes do not switch on one by one; they move in groups. The authors looked for gene groups whose joint activity stayed the same across species.

Those shared groups point to old, conserved rules for cell change. They guide stem cells as they pick a final cell type. Finding the shared rules could steady efforts to grow tissues in the lab. The paper treats evolution as a filter for what truly matters.
plos-pone-0003506:
Björn Friedrich and co-authors linked a gene variant to insulin release in this 2008 study. The gene, SGK1, makes a kinase switched on by serum and stress hormones. That kinase also plays roles in salt balance. Three European study groups took part in the work.

Variation in SGK1 tracked with differences in insulin secretion. The pattern appeared across the TUEF, EUGENE2, and METSIM studies. Consistent results across groups strengthen the claim. SGK1 now stands as a candidate gene for type 2 diabetes risk. Three groups agreeing makes a gene claim far harder to dismiss.
plos-pone-0003606:
Catherine J. Auger and Robin M. Forbes-Lorman studied a hormone's calming effect in male rats in this 2008 paper. Progesterone can reduce anxiety-like behavior in many animal tests. It acts by binding classic progestin receptors inside cells. Whether that route explains the calming effect was the question.

Their work tied the reduction in anxiety-like behavior to the progestin receptor. Blocking that receptor pathway changed the hormone's effect. A reproductive hormone thus steadies behavior through a named molecular route. The result clarifies how progesterone reaches the anxious brain. Anxiety disorders are very common. Calm without sedation is a long-sought goal for drug makers who study hormone routes like this one in male rats.
plos-pone-0003706:
Marybeth Langer, Alexander Malykhin, Kenichiro Maeda, and colleagues published this anthrax study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Inhaled anthrax can kill through runaway inflammation as much as through the germ itself. The authors suspected peptidoglycan, a mesh in the wall of Bacillus anthracis, of driving that response.

They purified the wall component and exposed human monocytes, a type of immune cell, to it. The peptidoglycan set off an inflammatory response through the p38 MAP kinase pathway. The finding names a bacterial building block behind the deadly inflammation of inhalation anthrax. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003806:
Mark B. Bain, Nuanchan Singkran, and Katherine E. Mills published this environmental study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Managing a great lake means juggling public interests, living ecosystems, and changing water conditions at a large scale. Lake Ontario's water levels are regulated, and each plan helps some users while hurting others.

The authors compared the impacts of seven water level management plans for the lake. Their integrated ecosystem assessment projects effects across ecological and human measures together. The framework shows how to run a great lake for people and nature at the same time.
plos-pone-0003906:
Soohyun Lee, Simon Kasif, Zhiping Weng, and co-authors examined gene data inside variable DNA regions in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns single-letter DNA changes called SNPs. Such markers are used widely in genetics and health studies. By habit, markers failing a balance test were thrown out of analyses.

The authors focus on regions where DNA copy counts differ between people. Extra or missing copies can make good markers look unbalanced. Their analysis warns against discarding markers in those regions too fast. The guidance helps genetics studies keep real signals they once dropped. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004006:
Xavier Gigandet, Patric Hagmann, Maciej Kurant, and co-authors weighed trust in MRI brain wiring maps in 2008. Diffusion MRI tractography draws the brain's white matter connections. Checking whether those drawn fibers are real remains hard. False connections could mislead both research and surgery.

Their PLOS ONE article proposes ways to estimate confidence in each connection. A confidence level tells users which links to trust most. That honesty makes tractography safer for clinical planning. It also helps brain network studies weigh strong and weak links. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004106:
Yuchuan Zhou, Min Zheng, Qixian Shi, and co-authors described a sperm protein from the epididymis in 2008. Sperm must mature in the epididymis before they can fertilize eggs. That final readiness step is called capacitation. Roles of epididymal proteins in the process were little known.

Their PLOS ONE article reports a secreted protein named HongrES1. It is made specifically in the epididymis of their study animals. The protein critically regulates capacitation and male fertility. Losing it impairs the sperm's ability to fertilize. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004206:
Valentina Mangano and colleagues published this malaria genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interferon regulatory factor 1 is a transcription factor with wide roles in the immune system's gene networks. It is a critical mediator of interferon gamma signalling and a major player in the response to infection.

Because of that record, the gene was a candidate for influencing severe malaria. The team tested it in child-parent trio studies across three African populations. They report a lack of association: the gene did not track with severe malaria. A clear negative result like this steers the search for malaria's genetic factors elsewhere.
plos-pone-0004306:
Anton Nikolaev and colleagues published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2009, the second of a pair. Retinal networks must adapt constantly to present the changing visual world to the brain at its best. In the companion paper, the team showed that adaptation improves how the fly eye represents naturalistic stimuli over time.

Here they test the hypothesis that this adaptation results from different mechanisms at several synaptic connections within the network. Working in the Drosophila eye, they separate the contributions of those connection points. The pair of papers shows a small eye solving a big problem: keeping vision sharp as light changes.
plos-pone-0004406: In 2009, a German team poisoned malaria's vitamin factory. Blocking a key vitamin enzyme targeted the malaria parasite. The germ's vital cofactor synthesis proved a weak point. The strategy opens a new antimalarial front. The enzyme differs sharply from the human version.
plos-pone-0004506: In 2009, a Colombian team found geometry in cancer's scaffolding. A tough fiber frame shaped a strange repeating pattern in tumors. The neat triangle patterns came back often. The finding maps tumor shape well today. The math behind it looks fractal.
plos-pone-0004606: In 2009, Guedj, Sébrié, and Rivals found green tea rescuing over-dosed brains. Green tea polyphenols rescued brain defects induced by DYRK1A overexpression. The tea compounds normalized brain development. The finding aids Down syndrome research greatly. The gene sits on HSA21.
plos-pone-0004706: In 2009, a team modeled drugs calming inflammation anew. In silico simulation of corticosteroid effects on an NFkB-dependent model was done. The drugs tamed the signaling storm quite well today. The model informs therapy design today. The immune pathways converge.
tourneur-revengers-tragedy-1606:
Printed in 1607 with no author's name, The Revenger's Tragedy was long credited to Cyril Tourneur. Most scholars now assign it to Thomas Middleton instead. Vindice, the lead figure, has spent nine years grieving for his murdered love, and he returns to court in disguise carrying her skull.

The court he enters is ruled by a lecherous Duke and a brood of grasping sons and stepsons. Plot piles on plot until revenge turns into a bloody masque of killing. Dark wit runs through every scene, and the mix of horror and sharp talk has made the play a lasting landmark of Jacobean drama.
acton-lectures-modern-history-1906:
Lord Acton lectured on modern history, and the 1906 volume gathers his survey from the Renaissance to the nineteenth century. Power, liberty, and conscience drive his account of how the modern world arose. Acton, a liberal Catholic, judged rulers by a strict moral code.

Famed for the line that power tends to corrupt, he weighs kings and churches alike. Nations rise, in his telling, as freedom gains or loses ground. The lectures show deep learning worn with clarity and force. Readers meet history as moral reasoning, taught by a master who believed the past must answer to conscience, not merely to success.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol1-1906:
G. R. S. Mead opens his great English Hermetica in Thrice-Greatest Hermes, Volume One, from 1906. Prolegomena come first: the history and meaning of the Hermetic writings. Mead, a Theosophical scholar, traces Hermes Trismegistus through Greek, Egyptian, and early Christian worlds with patient and loving erudition.

He asks who wrote the sermons and why they mattered so long. Pagan wisdom and church doctrine meet in his wide survey here. The edition brought Hermes to the modern English reader in full. This first volume is the doorway: a map and a history that prepare the reader for the sacred texts themselves in the volumes after.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol2-1906:
Sermons and fragments fill the second volume of Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes, from 1906. The divine Pymander and kindred wisdom discourses speak in Mead's clear English. Hermes instructs his son Tat and other seekers on God, mind, fate, and the soul's long road through the spheres to its home.

These mystical dialogues fed Renaissance magic for two centuries and more. Modern Theosophy drew on them just as eagerly in Mead's day. His notes guide the reader through hard symbols with care. The volume forms the heart of his edition, the Hermetic scriptures themselves, texts that shaped occult thought from Ficino to the present.
mead-thrice-greatest-hermes-vol3-1906:
Outlying pieces complete Mead's Thrice-Greatest Hermes in this third volume, from 1906. Excerpts, fragments, and testimonia gather around the core sermons here. Mead adds his full survey of Hermetic literature, mapping all that lies around and beyond the central texts of the tradition in Greek, Latin, and Arabic.

Scholars use the volume as a reference shelf for the whole Hermetic world. Lost books leave traces in these rescued scraps and citations. Mead's labor spared later students years of hunting through rare tomes. The full set remains the standard English gateway to Hermes Trismegistus, and this closing book is its index, attic, and treasure room in one.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-06:
One hard winter gives Volume 6, from 1897, its lasting fame. The book covers Quebec in 1633 and 1634 under Thwaites's editorship of the series. Le Jeune chose to spend the cold months with the Montagnais in the woods.

He shared their hunger, their fires, and their cramped tents for months. Frost, smoke, and scarce game mark his daily notes from camp. Two whole ways of seeing the world meet around one fire. Le Jeune writes with humor, grit, and rare respect for his hosts. The result ranks among the most vivid and human pages in all the Relations.
journal-of-discourses-vol-06:
Volume Six, from 1859, finds the Saints home again in their valley. A federal army camps in their midst, a daily test of patience. Young turns the discourses toward the hard work of consolidation.

Building the kingdom's farms, shops, and institutions fills the sermons' plans. Speakers urge self-reliance in food, cloth, and tools of every kind. Faith becomes statecraft, preached in the Tabernacle week by week here. The tone cools from war heat toward patient, daily construction. Readers watch a refuge turn into a lasting commonwealth in Utah's valleys. Patience, in these talks, counts as a form of warfare by other means.
virginia-charter-1606:
King James I granted the First Charter of Virginia in 1606 to a group of London merchants and gentlemen. Their company planned to plant an English colony on the coast of North America. The charter gave them legal cover to sail, settle, and govern under English law.

The text sets the colony's borders, names its ruling councils, and promises settlers the rights of English subjects. It also claims rights to mine gold, silver, and copper, sharing a part with the crown. A year later the company's colonists founded Jamestown. The charter is thus a founding paper of English America.
cia-0000008006:
November 1950 brought a CIA survey of Indochina's current situation and its probable course. France's fight against the Viet Minh was in its fourth year, and communist China had just won its own civil war. That victory raised the stakes along Vietnam's northern border.

The paper takes stock of French forces, Viet Minh strength, and local politics across Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. It stands near the start of formal American analysis of the region. Later US policy grew from readings like this one, made when involvement was still mostly money and advice. The file marks an early page in that story.
cia-0000009706:
How non-American prisoners were treated in Viet Cong detention camps is studied in an August 1971 CIA paper. Most prisoners in the southern system were South Vietnamese soldiers and officials, not Americans. Their numbers ran into the thousands, and their stories were less often told.

A treatment study would weigh food, labor, punishment, and release chances as sources reported them. Such knowledge served both humane concern and hard planning about the enemy's system. The paper widens the captivity record beyond its American center. It preserves evidence that the prison war's largest group of victims was Vietnamese.
cia-0000009906:
Three United States Air Force pilots were imprisoned together, and another died, a September 1967 report covers. The heading joins the two facts in one breath, as the event likely joined them. Aircrews captured together often stayed together through the prison system.

Companions in captivity could confirm each other's survival across years of silence. When one of a group died, the others' accounts became his record. Officials therefore valued group reports for the cross-checks they allowed later. This file opens three prisoner cases and closes a fourth, all from a single reported incident in the autumn of 1967.
cia-0000012306:
An undated Helms memo to the Director of Central Intelligence, its year estimated as 1962, carries the Penkovsky correspondence into the crisis year. That year would define the colonel's legacy, when his reporting on Soviet missiles faced its supreme test over Cuba. The memo's missing date is itself a small clue to the hurried paperwork of those months.

The letter belongs to the prelude: the tense season before the world learned how close it had come. Its summit address shows the case still commanding the top. For readers, it is one of the floating pages that drift through the files, dated by context.
cia-0000012406:
Yoga was the cryptonym for the Penkovsky meetings' summer phase, and a record opens its second phase in London across July and August 1961. The colonel was back in the chair after weeks in Moscow. Summer sessions resumed the questioning where spring had left it, with new tasking answered and new material delivered from inside the Soviet military.

The summer phase proved as productive as the spring's, if less frantic. Its records run under the Yoga heading through the season. For readers, the page opens the operation's second act: the same source, the same city, and higher stakes.
cia-0000013606:
Panama's gathering crisis fills a CIA paper from October 1968, titled simply the situation in Panama. The isthmus was sliding toward a change of power that autumn. The National Guard's officers were biding their time as the elected government wobbled. Within days, the Guard seized power in a coup. It began the military rule that lasted two decades, under the commander the analysts were already marking in these pages.

The paper covers the storm as it gathered over the canal republic. It weighs the guard's ambitions against the politicians' weakness. For readers, it shows a coup being foreseen in outline, in the files of the power that owned the canal.
cia-0000013906: Official Viet Cong policy on prisoner treatment did not always match local feeling, and a CIA report dated November 3, 1967, takes up that gap. Orders from above could soften or harden as they reached a camp. The report weighs the clash between the written line and real views. That clash helps explain why camp life varied so much.
cia-0000015306: A letter to Donald Keyhoe from J. S. Harmon fills a CIA file dated March 5, 1958. Harmon thanks Keyhoe for his letter of March 1. Keyhoe kept up a steady stream of demands for the truth on saucers. Polite thanks and no new facts was the reply he most often got. The Harmon reply is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000022306: General Carter called a meeting to discuss Gary Powers' proposed writings, a CIA record dated May 5, 1962, reports. Marshall Carter was then the agency's deputy director. Powers, newly freed in a spy swap, had a book in mind, and his old employer cared what he wrote. The meeting shows the agency managing the story of its own pilot.
cia-0000039306:
Case number 12517 receives its photo comparison results in a CIA record dated November 5, 1970. An attached memo also mentions Thomas H. Pilkington in connection with the case. The record belongs to the MIA and POW identification work of the Vietnam War.

Inside are the findings for the numbered case, with the memo adding its own notes. Attached memos often carried the context that the bare result left out. Together they show how a single case file could hold two things at once. It held a laboratory judgment and the office discussion around it. Both were preserved on the same few pages for later readers.
cia-0000044506:
The archbishop supported the Jesuit position on the killing probe, in a CIA record dated April 6, 1990. By spring the probe had run for months without satisfying its critics. Church support gave the Jesuits' stance public and moral backing.

Inside, the archbishop's backing of the order's position is recorded. The Jesuits had pressed for a fuller and braver investigation. Standing with them cost the archbishop ease with the government. He accepted that cost in public, which his office rarely did without great cause. The file shows the church holding together under that strain, months after the murders, when public attention had moved on and steady pressure mattered most.
cia-0000044906:
Chile's FPMR issued a communique on the Haeberle kidnapping, in a CIA record dated July 2, 1986. The FPMR was an armed group fighting the Pinochet regime. A communique announcing a kidnapping was its claim of responsibility.

Inside, the group's statement on the seizure is preserved as issued. Urban guerrillas used such claims to prove they could still strike. Each one was read closely by the regime and by foreign watchers. A kidnapping claim announced reach, planning, and a safe house somewhere in the capital. The file holds the group's voice from 1986, in a long campaign of raids and seizures waged against a dictatorship that answered in kind.
cia-0000045206:
AFP reported that the mayor of Santo Domingo was asked to mediate in the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Outside mediators were sought when direct talks stalled or burned. A mayor from the Dominican Republic was an unusual choice of broker.

Inside, the mediation appeal is recorded as the wire reported it. Bringing in a third party admits that the two sides cannot finish alone. It also widens the circle of people who know the talks' secrets. The file preserves the appeal at its making, a sign of how far the search for a trusted middleman had ranged that September.
cia-0000049006: The Salvadoran left planned burials for its six assassinated FDR leaders in 1980, and a CIA item from that year preserves the plans. The FDR was the political front allied with the guerrillas, and its leaders had been seized and murdered that November. In that war, funerals were demonstrations, and the plans show mourning being organized as protest.
cia-0000049206: A partly blacked-out CIA item from 1991 reports improvement in human rights abuses by the Salvadoran air force. Improvement was the word certification season ran on: each claimed step forward argued for continued American aid. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where such claims were later checked against the dead.
cia-0000049306: The investigation of the Jesuit murders had stalled by 1990, and a CIA item from that year records the stall, kept with the Truth Commission records. A stalled case was not a dead one: pressure could restart it, and everyone in the file knew that too. The item preserves the pause that the case's friends refused to accept.
cia-0000049406: Election outlook in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049406, dated February 2, 1984. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and looks ahead to a Salvadoran vote. Readers find a short declassified forecast item whose title states its purpose, part of the agency's regular political reporting on El Salvador during the war years.
cia-0000095206: A cable to Leopoldville about Congo covert action against an unidentified high official is declassified CIA document 0000095206, dated July 6, 1960. The target is described only as an unidentified high official. Readers get a short declassified cable record from the Congo's independence summer, its heading stating the action type while withholding the person's name.

plos-pone-0005406: Angiotensin II damages kidneys, but its cousin may protect. Esteban and team show angiotensin-(1-7) and its Mas sensor are key players in renal swelling, with Mas deficiency reducing damage. The axis offers healing angles. The kidney's own balancing system revealed.
plos-pone-0005506: Mud snail embryos reveal how timing evolves. Goulding traced cell lineage in Ilyanassa beyond the 29-cell stage, finding accelerated regional differentiation. plos-pone-0006606: A factor mix brews dopamine neurons. Vazin and team found the SPIE mix drives dopamine neuron growth from human stem cells. The recipe beats older methods — brain cells, bottled, for therapy, with SDIA beaten. PA6 and MS5 lines: molecular nature probed.
plos-pone-0009406: The gut absorbs food through a forest of microscopic fingers called microvilli, packed in perfect hexagonal rows. plos-pone-0009506: The Indus script, from a Bronze Age civilization, remains undeciphered. This paper applies n-gram statistics — counting how symbol sequences pattern — to probe whether the mysterious signs behave like a real writing system. plos-pone-0009606: When a newborn is starved of oxygen, doctors lack good tests to track the damage and recovery. plos-pone-0010606: JC virus's small t antigen hijacks cell-cycle controls to copy viral DNA. This study shows it binds PP2A and Rb-family proteins and is needed for efficient replication. The paper details a viral takeover mechanism. The mechanism reveals how a quiet virus seizes control.
plos-pone-0010706: Stem cells respond to signals only at the right moment. This study finds differentiating embryonic stem cells pass through temporal windows of responsiveness. The paper maps when cells listen. The timing insight will guide future regenerative medicine protocols using stem cells.
